Name: 4_little birds_horses_horse_poor parish
Representative_Docs:
['When I walked through the oak forest, drowsiness overcame me; and by morning, rosemary had blossomed behind my head. I cut all the green rosemary twigs, set them afloat on the water, on the cold water. The maiden who will catch the green rosemary will be my dearest by the cold water. The maidens went to the river in the morning, filling buckets: then those rosemary twigs were floating right to the footbridge. Anička, the miller’s daughter, leaned over the twigs and, unfortunate little dove, fell into the water. 

1) Bells ring, bells ring three times, what could that mean? Tell me, you little birds! Surely it’s not my beloved? "Your beloved, your joy, they are laying in a coffin; four men in black robes are putting her in the grave." 

Ah, my dearest God! You have taken my bride from me! Tell me, you little birds, the way to her grave. "Behind the hill, in the little church, priests are singing in the choir; five steps behind the little church, in the grave, lies your beloved." 

There I will go, I will weep, I will sit on that dark grave, and for you, my maiden, I will bear a heavy sorrow. I will bear the heavy sorrow until death frees me, and a wreath of rosemary will be laid on my shroud!', 'Oh, this poor Tapa parish,  
The hungry Näu village,  
Where I don’t dare to walk in the manor,  
I don’t flash before the lord:  
I don’t even have a barley cake in my pocket,  
Nor any oat porridge in my pan.  
Salt is scarce inside the box,  
And beer is thin in the neck.  
Women walk the manor roads  
Wearing egg mittens.  
Pairs of chickens in the stall,  
Pairs of geese under the hem.  
Thread scarves in their hands,  
The court’s sheep on the hilltop  
Are led out into the manor yard  
To the old lord on the rampart.  
From there the lord comes grunting:  
“Look where the poor sheep stands.  
Take it home to the dogs,  
Give it to the hound!  
Bring me a fatty from the barn,  
A pretty one from the herd  
To carry to the manor’s sheepfold.”  
When the people go to work:  
The coachman goes like a devil,  
The young lord like Judas behind;  
The parish like a prisoner in the middle.  
Then you hear the coachman’s voice,  
The old lord’s cursing.  
There the rowan struggles,  
And then the fir tree moves  
And there the bird cherry staggers  
Over the shoulder of the apple tree.  
But it strikes past the fine coat,  
Past the thin shoulders,  
Past the long sleeves.  
The tenant sighs in slave bondage,  
A tear in his eye.  
The coachman is called hell,  
The young lord is sent after,  
The old lord to watch.  
Tables are set in place,  
Chairs are brought to the table,  
Fire and tar also brought:  
Eat, coachman, drink, steward,  
This poor parish’s toil,  
Its tiny pain-blood.  
If you tormented the parish,  
If you tormented the little ones.  
Oh, this golden Kuruda,  
Silver Roosnaida,  
When the people went to work:  
The coachman like the moon,  
The young lord like God behind,  
The parish like copper in the middle.  
No fir moves there,  
Nor does the rowan struggle.  
No bird cherry staggers there,  
Over the shoulder of the apple tree.  
No sound of the coachman’s voice,  
Nor the steward’s whining,  
Nor the old lord’s cursing.', 'I was a slave, I tended the herd  
I was in the Dutch service  
In the fields of Lehila's sheep  
Holland made a new dome  
Lehila land a wide coat.  
Oh, poor me, a prisoner of children  
Complained from the hiding place!  
Nights I am imprisoned, nights I am saved.  
Nights I keep watch over my father’s herd  
I protect the herd of my brother  
At the river mouth, at the lake mouth  
In the middle of the river’s whirlpool  
Between the river’s currents.  
Two merchants came  
Two merchant servants  
Both had swords at their belts  
Both had spurs on their feet.  
"Maiden, young girl  
In embroidered clothing, slender,  
Sell me father’s horse  
Trade for brother’s saddle."  
"I will not sell father’s herd  
I will not trade brother’s saddle  
Father has a good horse,  
Brother has a dear saddle."  
"Sell me the sword at your belt  
Trade for the spurs on your feet."  
"I will not sell the sword at my belt  
I will not trade the spurs on my feet  
Maiden, young girl  
Allow me to come to you,  
To come to you until death  
To be with you until the end of life.  
I will put you to easy work:  
Beating rye stalks  
Treading on oat husks.  
In summer I keep smoke away  
In winter I lift dust away.  
In summer I feed you sugar rushes  
In winter buckwheat tangles,  
A year's goose meat.  
I protect the herd with walnut cores."  
"I hear, I answer:  
Salt cellars you have for sugar  
Pumpkins for goose meat."  
"Allow me to come  
To come to you, to stay with you."  
"Maybe you would bake me in gold  
Spin silk threads  
Sew with silver thread.  
Maybe there would be a silver yard  
An iron-forged gate  
Stone in the corral,  
Still I will not come to you.  
For you a pigsty  
A horse’s nightmare,  
A dog’s snout with a stick in it  
A mouth like a poor man’s hole  
Face like a paper sack  
Teeth like cattle gates  
Jaws like that of a tongs.  
I will go where it is created  
Where the Creator has made a place  
Mary has given a home.  
Where my blood has carried  
Where my color has taken me  
Where my little luck shares in.  
Maybe there would be an oily yard  
Maybe a fenced garden  
Gates forged from twigs,  
Maybe there would be a pillar in the yard  
In the corral stone stakes  
Still I go where it is created,  
Where the Creator has made a place,  
Mary has given a home.  
Where my blood has carried  
Where my color has taken me  
Where my little luck shares in."']

6. I will come there behind you on the millstone, there we will love each other until the break of day.', 'Ehehe, there’s a partner for the lunchbox and a partner for superstition too,

Bigger bones die

Long backs weaken', 'What was hell for ages past,  
That was in our manor too,  
Oxen trample the fields,

Ploughs between the shafts.

Women weep by the doors.  
Hold the mitten in hand,

For the German soldiers’ march.', 'Oh, this ace of a gentleman

Name: 8_bride_wedding_maidens_marriage
Representative_Docs:
['1.  
Hey, see the Bride, ribbon band with ornaments,  
Encircled with maiden faith,  
Longs to soon satisfy her desires.  
She blushes and the green turns dull!  
Well Nymphs, quickly, want to spread her the coach!  
Expose the bed of fresh green!  
Let these two there satisfy their desires,  
Quietly with their kisses.

2.  
But hold, say, don’t let him come so quickly  
To his beloved Bride!  
These lessons must first be properly taken:  
Bind him out of the room  
As long as he does not promise your sweet request  
Or whatever you desire for sweetness.  
If he promises it, hey, the maidenhood is worth  
The little pussy’s flesh.

3.  
If the pair is in bed, then no need is lost.  
Every couple sharpens their minds:  
Here is the right hour born of joy!  
What a playful handclap!  
Quiet, be still, the playmates will say it!  
Those are two breasts full of spirit  
That will well lay the entry of the joy of the feast.', "Tiny Cupid, you have with Pyle snoo,  
Requested a lover so, and have won his heart and ground,  
Quite dearly won,  
Who is struck by you in the sun,  
Whereby a lover comes to the joy of love,  
He does not regret, that he has asked for it.  
It is sweet love, which like a hot ember,  
For the pleasant mind: Boost her faithful mind,  
And the heart and mind are united,  
And have received a mutual love from her,  
That was what truly fulfilled your desire,  
And that you would live as man and wife.  
Now be joyful, and create full delight,  
You who in honor and virtue are gathered together,  
Joined by love's bond,  
So wedding guests now want to be merry,  
And drink once the chosen health,  
A Rumor wine, it shall be the health.  
Everyone from the bride and bridegroom drinks,  
A good fresh flute,  
Playmates now do not dream,  
And playing servants do not hesitate,  
When you lay the bride to the wedding bed,  
So take care that she does not slip from you,  
But fair and neat, properly closed the door.", "We feel like singing the praise,
Of the necessary things,
Of marriage, or the power of the land,
So joyful! Our cat has kittens!
If I had now a hundred thousand tongues,
And Lord Rosthuizer his mind!
How would I, through my poetry,
Teach this lovely pair of doves to tumble!
But listen, this little herb does not move me,
Or sawing branches in the bride's garden,
Or ambushing the finch with a net.
That is best done where no one sees.
The honking of the geese, and the cackling,
Of the hen, are his oracles,
And wondrous spells of Apollo,
Full of liver veins, throats of blowholes,
Latin decorates the apothecary's pots,
Just as the miller adorns the beautiful face.
But holla, hold on ... that serpent of serpents,
Also makes my wrong nuts crack;
I had to lament about true matrimony.
And how the wives, to please,
Bear the world of the husband,
So that it does not perish.
That great porter of the globe,
At our Town Hall, is just a little egg
In the number laughed at by the woman,
Who from evening till morning:
Will care for the world's durability,
And strives for the increase of the people.
Marriage is an old custom
For Adam had a wife out of necessity;
But tell me, how would that go,
If one had to do without the female sex?
Who then would, to gather people,
Ever beat the drum of marriage?
If the female sex also had to live alone,
(Like the poets separate the Amazons,
Sorted apart from the men)
Then it would be best to create the man.
Completely defenseless and without weapons.
Who then cares for the rose wreath?
An Amazon (so to speak)
Is but a bench without a blanket,
And a little candlestick without a candle.
A little field that remains fallow."]
